chapter: Touring, recording and Fletcher's band in the 1940s
title: John Hammond finances raiding Nat Towles' Omaha band
summary: Hammond had Horace, Israel Crosby and Emmett Berry fly to Omaha, where they took men from Nat Towles' band, rehearsed two weeks on Hammond's money, then recorded in New York. Drummer Debo Mills sang a blues to his wife, bandleader Anna Mae Winburn.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: I also have here that in early -- or no, in December of 1940, that you got the band together again. Apparently, there had been a time when you didn't have the band, and this time you were using personnel from Nat Towles -- is that it -- or Towles? I'm not familiar with that --
There was a band leader, a big guy, named Nat Towles out of Omaha, Nebraska. He had some excellent musicians with him.

I don't think there was anybody that was too famous. Yes, I'll take that back. There was a guy named Harold Johnson that's with Duke Ellington's son's band now. We call him Money Johnson. Now he was out of Nat Towles' band, and he was just through here recently, in Denver, and played the Warehouse, and I talked with him. Now he was also a member of -- you remember a guy that had a band named Bull Moose Jackson?

Harold Johnson was in that band, in Los Angeles. And Nat Towles had some great musicians. Another guy named Lee Pope, a very good saxophone player. Another excellent tenor saxophonist named Bob Dorsey. Man, he could play. He was a character, but he could play. And I'll tell you what happened. This has just come to me. There was a guy that always has been instrumental in helping musicians secure jobs, or get recordings for them, and he's always been a very good friend of mine, been very helpful to me. He was helpful to Fletcher as well as other musicians. John Hammond.
Well, John Hammond was a lover of Israel Crosby the bassist in Chicago. Israel Crosby was in my

band. He also liked Emmett Barry, the great trumpet player. Well, John Hammond had me get Israel Crosby, Emmet Barry, and myself together. We flew out to Omaha, Nebraska, and -- I hate to say it -- we raided Nat Towles' band because he wasn't doing too much, but they could play, man. They were together. But we stayed in Omaha about two weeks, and I rehearsed in a house there where I was staying. John Hammond financed us this whole thing for me, and we got together and rehearsed, and he flew us to New York City to record us. I had a drummer named Debo Mills. We called him Danny Bo. Man, he could drum. He's one of the few drummers that could make triple beats on a bass drum at any tempo that you played. Clear. I mean clear. And there was a little story behind him.

There was an all girl revue band called the International Sweethearts of Rhythm. Well, the leader of this particular band was a girl named Anna May Winburn. Well, this was his wife, and -- I'm saying this to say that we made a recording in New York, and he sang also, and he sang some lyrics to Anna May, you know. It was a blues. It was a great thing, and the record sold pretty good.

But John Hammond, getting back to what he did for us, he came out to Omaha after I had kept him, you know, well -- what shall I say -- he wanted to know, let's put it this way, what was going on, and so after two weeks of rehearsing I was keeping him -- what's the word I want?

Informed. I'm a little off. I've been up all day today. He would be informed of just what was happening and how the band was progressing on the arrangements, and all, and he said because we want to come into New York and cut these sides, and after I'd thought that the band was well rehearsed and we had the arrangements down under our fingers, so to speak, I called John up and I said, "John, I think we're ready." So he flew out, and he heard them, and he said, "Yeah, you are ready." So he took us to New York, took the whole bill, got us -- the whole band -- rooms in a hotel there, and we went down and we recorded.
This was when? Do you recall?
You had something there (inaudible) about Nat Towles; It was during that era.
